title: Two Friends, a Disused Petrol Station and a $5 Ice-Cream Course
dek: In May 1978 two 27-year-olds who felt they had failed at everything opened an ice-cream shop in a run-down Burlington petrol station, not expecting it to last a year.

story.event: Opening an ice-cream shop in a renovated gas station in Burlington, Vermont
story.summary: On 5 May 1978 Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, childhood friends who had taken a $5 Penn State correspondence course in ice-cream making, opened Ben & Jerry's Homemade in a run-down gas station in Burlington, Vermont, with $12,000, of which $4,000 was a bank loan. They had dropped a bagel plan because the equipment cost too much, and expected so little that they promised free ice cream if they survived a year; the first Free Cone Day was held in 1979.
paragraphs: On 5 May 1978, people queued outside a renovated petrol station in Burlington, Vermont, for the opening of Ben & Jerry's Homemade. Its owners, Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield, were 27, childhood friends from Long Island, and neither had run a business. Greenfield had been turned down by medical schools; Cohen had been driving his pottery to craft fairs and, by his account, selling almost none of it. "There we were, failing at everything we were trying to do," Greenfield later recalled.

They settled on food because they liked eating. Bagels came first, until the used equipment turned out to cost about $40,000, by Cohen's reckoning, far more than they had. Ice cream looked cheaper. They split a $5 correspondence course from Penn State, whose tests were open book. For a town they wanted somewhere with students and no ice-cream parlour, and chose Burlington. Their money was $12,000: $4,000 from each of them, half of Cohen's share from his father, and $4,000 borrowed from a bank.

What they could afford was a run-down petrol station across from City Hall Park, with parking where the pumps had been. Cohen remembered inches of ice on the floor. They fitted it out with secondhand ice-cream makers and the cheapest wood they could find, and Cohen made the shop's bowls, plates and mugs himself; the glaze came out a blue he later called ugly. Alongside the ice cream they sold soup and crêpes. They did not expect to last. Cohen later said they thought the odds of surviving a year were slim, so they promised free ice cream for everyone if they reached their first anniversary. The plan, he said, was to sell the shop after a few years and become long-distance lorry drivers.

They reached it. In May 1979 they held the first Free Cone Day, free scoops all day, which the company still runs. That year they dropped the crêpes and began selling wholesale; in 1980 they rented space in an old spool and bobbin mill to pack pints, which Cohen delivered from the back of his Volkswagen. By 1987 Ben & Jerry's was a $30 million business selling in 35 states. The petrol station was knocked down for a car park in 1982.

quote.text: Now as to your five-bushel gourd, why did you not make a boat of it, and float about over river and lake? You could not then have complained of its not holding anything!
quote.source_title: Chuang Tzŭ: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer, tr. Herbert A. Giles, Project Gutenberg eBook #59709
quote.connection: Hui Tzŭ smashed his huge gourd because it made a poor water jar; Zhuangzi told him he should have floated on it. Cohen and Greenfield did something similar with a dead petrol station, a struggling potter's bowls and a five-dollar course, judging each by what it might become rather than what it was meant for.

reflection: Nothing in this story began as the right tool. The building had stopped being a petrol station, the pottery had not sold, the course cost five dollars, and the founders expected to be gone within a year. Zhuangzi's complaint about the gourd was that its owner judged it only by the use he had in mind.
You probably carry a few things that did not work out the way you meant them to: a skill from a job you left, a plan that stalled, a tool built for something else. Some of them may float.
invitation: Write down one thing you have that failed at its first purpose: a skill, a draft, a contact or a piece of equipment. Spend five minutes asking what else it could be for, then leave the question there.

cross_checks.claim: The first shop opened on 5 May 1978 in a renovated gas station in Burlington, Vermont
They dropped a bagel plan because the equipment cost more than they had, and took a $5 Penn State correspondence course
They started with $12,000: $4,000 from each founder and $4,000 borrowed from a bank
Burlington was chosen as a college town without an ice-cream parlour
The first Free Cone Day was held on the first anniversary in 1979
The shop also sold soup and crêpes, dropped in 1979
By 1987 Ben & Jerry's was a $30 million business selling in 35 states

research_notes: Start-up money: Cohen (Studio Potter, 1990), the company timeline, TIME, CNBC and HISTORY.com all give $12,000 made up of $4,000 from each founder and $4,000 borrowed; Entrepreneur says $8,000 of their own money and $4,000 borrowed (same split); but student-newspaper reports of Greenfield's lectures (The Signal 2016, and Oakland Post) speak of an $8,000 bank loan. The story uses the version given by Cohen himself and the company. Bagel equipment: Cohen in 1990 put it at $40,000; Greenfield (via CNBC, from The Washington Post) said only that it was more than they had; the story attributes the figure to Cohen. Greenfield's rejections: CNBC says he did not get into medical school, Pipe Dream reports 'not once, but twice', The Signal 'every medical school to which he applied'; the story says he had been turned down by medical schools. Cohen's 'never sold any' pots is his own hyperbole; the story says 'almost none'. The Washington Post interview (2014) quoted by CNBC and Tasting Table is paywalled, so it is not cited directly; Cohen's description of the gas station and the ice on the floor are taken from Tasting Table's quotation of it, and the 'odds ... were slim' remark from CNBC's quotation of the Boston Phoenix (2003). The 'used' ice-cream makers and cheap wood come from Pipe Dream's report of a Greenfield talk (it says World War II-era makers and green wood); Cohen in 1990 mentions an old-fashioned rock-salt ice-cream maker. The story uses British 'petrol station' and 'lorry drivers' in its own prose; the company's records say gas station. The Zhuangzi passage is from the authentic inner chapters; Giles's note reads it as a lesson that a thing's worth depends on how it is applied.
